papers.summary: BMuon changes Muon’s geometry to favor channel pruning. In a 1B language model, it preserves perplexity through 80% MLP-channel pruning, but its unpruned perplexity is worse than Muon’s (12.84 versus 10.92).
papers.relevance: Direct test of whether training improves compressibility while preserving quality, though the compression is structured channel pruning rather than low-rank factorization.

evidence.quote: On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning.
BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking.

papers.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility

papers.summary: Monarch–Muon trains structured weights with matrix-aware updates. Its matched-structure quality runs improve on Monarch–AdamW, while separate 6.89B-reference systems measurements report 52.94 versus 68.87 GB peak memory and 1638.6 versus 2986.9 ms full-step time against dense Muon.
papers.relevance: Addresses the quality, memory, and throughput tradeoff of compressed parameterizations in pretraining.
papers.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining

papers.summary: Ori tracks drifting gradient subspaces for low-rank LLM pretraining. At rank 16 on a 130M model, reported validation perplexity is 43.61 versus GaLore’s 60.29. Its 1B rank-32 optimizer-step peak memory is 0.2487 GB versus GaLore’s 0.3385 GB.
papers.relevance: Directly informs low-rank gradient optimization under stringent memory constraints.

evidence.quote: when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05).
at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB).

papers.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training

papers.summary: A theoretical account of why trace-norm-regularized adaptation can have low-rank global minimizers: frozen activations create a finite-rank observation bottleneck. It also relates balanced LoRA weight decay to nuclear-norm regularization, but does not rule out spurious local minima.
papers.relevance: Closely matches nuclear-norm regularization and the geometry of low-rank fine-tuning.

evidence.quote: Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output.
By the standard equivalence between nuclear-norm regularization and balanced weight decay
This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation.

papers.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape

papers.summary: DT-LoRA refreshes a dynamic branch using principal residual-gradient directions outside the current LoRA tangent space. On GLUE, it reports an 88.7 average, 1.1 points above LoRA at the same parameter budget; the measured iteration time is 0.89 seconds, 70 ms above LoRA.
papers.relevance: Combines LoRA optimization geometry with practical fine-tuning and runtime measurements.

evidence.quote: On GLUE ( Tab. 6 ), DT-LoRA achieves the highest average score of 88.7, outperforming LoRA under the same parameter budget by 1.1 points
With τ = 5 \tau=5 , it requires 0.89 0.89 s per iteration, only 70 70 ms more than LoRA

papers.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation

papers.summary: For separable linear classification, the paper proves that fixed finite Newton–Schulz iterations plus positive stabilization change Muon’s asymptotic selection from spectral to Frobenius max-margin. The result does not establish the same behavior for stochastic LLM training.
papers.relevance: Directly addresses how practical Newton–Schulz approximations alter spectral optimization bias.

evidence.quote: Muon with a fixed number of Newton-Schulz iterations and positive stabilization leads to Frobenius max-margin selection on linear classification problems.
Our results focus on full-batch linear classification, leaving stochastic optimization and nonlinear neural networks beyond the present analysis.

papers.title: From Spectral to Frobenius: When Muon Loses Its Spectral Implicit Bias

papers.summary: Fine-tuning updates can have a few strong singular directions and a long tail. Across 13 released model pairs, different rank measures give sharply different impressions relative to shape-matched noise; the paper argues that rank claims need a noise baseline.
papers.relevance: A methodological check on using effective rank or singular spectra as proxies for useful low-rank compressibility.

evidence.quote: the updates have a few strong directions and a long tail that holds most of the energy.
report any rank measure of a weight update next to its value on a random matrix of the same shape

papers.title: Rank Measures of Fine-Tuning Updates Need a Noise Baseline

limitations: BMuon studies channel pruning, not low-rank weight factorization, and sacrifices unpruned language-model quality.
Monarch–Muon’s large-model memory and speed measurements are systems benchmarks separate from its complete quality runs; projection-method timings exclude periodic refreshes.
Ori’s cited memory figure measures the additional peak during the optimizer step, not total training memory.
The LoRA bottleneck paper is primarily theoretical; the retrieved evidence does not establish practical fine-tuning gains.
DT-LoRA’s cited timing does not establish end-to-end memory savings.
The Muon implicit-bias theorem is limited to full-batch linear classification.
Rank concentration alone does not establish retained model quality after low-rank compression.
